particularites.text: Offset fiscal year: Copart closes its fiscal year on 31 July, not in December. The years in the table denote fiscal years (e.g. 'FY2025' = year ended 31 July 2025), not calendar years - handled by the fyEndMonth=7 field.

No dividend paid despite a largely positive net cash position: a deliberate and structural capital allocation choice (high-ROIC land, reserve for opportunism/catastrophes, opportunistic buybacks). The buyback has been active again since Q2 FY2026 (>1,6 Md$ over 9 months) after several years at $0; the new CEO (Jay Adair, returning on 31/07/2026) signals a diversification of capital towards M&A and organic investment on top of buybacks (call of 06/07/2026) - the future buyback pace is therefore uncertain, see hypothese/ancrages.

compliance.note: No proven fraud and no allegation by an activist analyst/short seller (Muddy Waters, Hindenburg, Citron type) identified in the stock's history to date. The only item recorded (see items) is an investigation solicitation by plaintiff law firms - a preliminary stage and a common one after any material share price decline in the US, with no formally filed complaint and no proven element of fraud at this stage (search of 2026-08-09: still no formal complaint filed, status unchanged). The stock's ordinary commercial/employment litigation is outside the scope of this section.

clesRetenues: Q Bob Labick (CJS Securities) - macro factors to watch for a recovery in volumes: Liaw points to the cyclicality of insurance premium/rate growth, insurers with healthier income statements being able to reinvest in marketing/competitive pricing once consumer purchasing habits normalise.

Q Bob Labick - returns/results from the ramp-up of the sales force: Liaw stresses that the investments cover commercial, product and technology capabilities beyond sales headcount alone, each spend assessed individually rather than an overall SG&A ratio.

Q Craig Kennison (Baird) - future land capacity needs: Stearns explains that faster cycles allow more efficient use of land, disciplined case-by-case analysis, land investment expected to continue over the coming decade.

Q Craig Kennison - risk of disruption by AI: Liaw highlights physical storage, the global buyer network, the established platform and regulatory expertise as durable moats, priority given to internal AI deployment to preserve the competitive advantage.
Q Bret Jordan (Jefferies) - intensifying price competition: Liaw refocuses the topic on the 'economic outcome delivered' rather than price, vehicle selling price gaps far outweighing fee gaps.
Q Bret Jordan - performance of Copart Dealer Services (CDS): Stearns reports 5% unit volume growth year on year with expansion of the dealer user base.

Q John Healy (Northcoast Research) - outlook for accident/total-loss frequency: Liaw explains that accident frequency is declining structurally (vehicle safety) but that total-loss frequency offsets this through the ageing of the fleet and 'risk homeostasis' behaviours.

Q John Healy - why buybacks now rather than another capital allocation: Liaw cites valuation multiples, interest rates and relative positioning, no inside information beyond standard allocation discipline.

Q Jeffrey Lick (Stephens) - near-term impact of emerging technologies (EVs, autonomous driving, lease returns): Liaw indicates that this does not materially change 5-10 year investment decisions on capacity/technology, focus on leading indicators rather than short-term noise.

Q Jeffrey Lick - which catalyst would signal an inflection in volume growth: Liaw identifies cyclical factors (consumer insurance purchasing behaviour, insurer policy changes, non-insurance segments) - dynamic judged cyclical, not structural.

Q Jash Patwa (JPMorgan) - has the de-emphasis of low-value units disadvantaged volumes vs the industry: Stearns explains that units below 1 000$ are old/non-running, uninsured vehicles going through impound lots or staying with their owners, a fragmented market outside Copart's focus.

Q Jash Patwa - performance of the Purple Wave heavy equipment business: Liaw attributes the underperformance to customs tariff uncertainty disrupting the sector, organic investments in sales talent/platform maintained, M&A secondary to organic growth.

Q Jash Patwa - explanation of the sequential moderation in service margin: Stearns cites a one-off international VAT accrual of 6,8 M$; excluding catastrophe units and that item, margins improve markedly year on year.

Q Bob Labick (CJS Securities) - pass-through of fuel cost in the hybrid towing model: Liaw explains that Copart runs its own fleet, supports contractors through structured leasing/towing programmes, and adjusts rates market by market to preserve the service level and contractor profitability.

Q Bob Labick - impact of the decline in SAAR (annualised new vehicle sales rate) since 2020 on future salvage volumes: Liaw replies that Copart's supply comes from a layer of more than 10 years of vehicles already on the road, not from the timing of fleet entry - what matters is miles driven and the accident rate, not the build date.

Q Bob Labick - 5-year growth drivers: Liaw cites (1) the rise in insurance total-loss frequency, (2) the expansion of non-insurance volumes (rental/dealers/fleets/finance), (3) international expansion, (4) actively promoting a higher total-loss frequency through better returns for insurers, (5) ecosystem services reducing friction.

Q Craig Kennison (Baird) - insurer partners' outlook for 2026-2027: Liaw indicates that insurers are seeing consumers pulling back (~1 policyholder in 6 has reduced coverage), acknowledge cyclical trends, and expect major discussions on AI deployment - Copart highlights its AI capabilities on claims.

Q Craig Kennison - drivers of the 18% growth in international service revenue: Stearns cites strong performance in the United Kingdom, Germany and Canada, with Germany showing particular progress as insurers adopt the Copart-style total-loss remarketing model, improving volumes and profitability.

Q Jash Patwa (JPMorgan) - size of the non-insurance business and profile of cross-over buyers: Liaw describes buyers discovering Copart via search/social media for a specific vehicle, then broadening into adjacent categories in concentric circles, from damaged rental vehicles towards better-condition inventory.

Q Jash Patwa - is the pure sale (no reserve price) mix contractual or dynamic: Liaw confirms that it is non-contractual - insurers move to pure sales voluntarily as they observe Copart's liquidity, a reserve price would chill participation.

Q Jash Patwa - breakdown of revenue per unit (RPU) growth between ASP, mix and initiatives such as Title Express: Liaw cites Title Express penetration (processing 6-8x more volume than competitors), higher selling prices shared with Copart, volume growth, and the non-insurance seller mix (premium pricing).

Q John Healy (Northcoast Research) - definition and size of the whole car business, seller composition (including hail vehicles): Liaw describes a spectrum running from total-loss to near-new vehicles, Copart winning rights progressively (rental/damaged trade-ins then better-condition fleet vehicles).

Q John Healy - Purple Wave performance and investment in the business: Stearns reports Purple Wave GTV up more than 25% year on year, driven by territorial expansion and enterprise account development, team 2,5-3x larger than at acquisition.

Q Jeff Lick (Stephens) - long-distance delivery product: Stearns explains that it reduces friction and brings cost certainty to buyers, generating ~15 M$ of additional operating cost year on year with attractive margins and strong adoption.
Q Jeff Lick - clarification of pure sale vs sale without reserve: Liaw confirms that pure sale is synonymous with a sale with no reserve price.

pointsCles: Q3 FY26 revenue of 1,237 Md$ (+2,1% y/y), net income almost flat (402,4 M$, -1,0%) but EPS up (+2,4% to 0,43$) thanks to buybacks - at the scale of the first 9 months of FY26, cumulative net income is perfectly flat (1 156,8 M$ vs 1 156,0 M$ a year earlier, +0,07%) and cumulative EPS almost flat (+0,8%), the strong Q1 (+11,7% EPS) having been erased by a weak Q2 (-10,0% EPS, unfavourable CAT comp).

US insurance unit volumes down (-4,2% y/y) on the back of lower claims frequency - a headwind judged cyclical by management, offset by the rise in average selling prices (+4,6% overall, a seasonal record in Q3) and by international (+5,9% in units, +14,1% in revenue).

Buybacks: 43,4 M shares retired for >1,6 Md$ over the first 9 months of FY26 (average price ~37$/share) via 10b5-1 + open market - first year of buyback since at least FY2021 (buyback at 0$ in each year FY2021-FY2025, verified). Liquidity at end-Q3: 5,5 Md$ (of which 4,2 Md$ cash + HTM securities), zero debt.

Management transition: Jay Adair takes back the CEO role on 31/07/2026 (Jeff Liaw becomes special adviser). On a special call on 06/07/2026 (first call outside a quarterly release in 32 years), Adair signalled a slowdown in land capex (~500 M$/yr historically) and a redirection of capital towards M&A and organic investment (international, domestic whole car, technology), on top of buybacks - the future buyback pace is therefore no longer guaranteed at the Q2-Q3 FY26 level.

hypothese.summary: World leader in online auctions of total-loss/salvage vehicles, with an exceptional physical and technological moat; in a cyclical air pocket confirmed over 9 months (FY26 net income almost flat, not growing) and a competitive one (return of IAA under RB Global), offset by pricing. FY26 revenue/margin/EPS rebuilt bottom-up on the 9 actual months (not an extrapolation); the 2027-2030 recovery ramp made gradual as a consequence.
hypothese.text:
== THESIS SUMMARY ==
Copart is the dominant US salvage-auction intermediary (~50% share, duopoly with RB Global ~35%) with one of the cleanest moats in the portfolio: ~280 physical yards operating as local monopolies, self-reinforcing auction liquidity, and a twenty-year technology lead since the 2003 all-digital pivot - operating margins ~37%, exceptional cash conversion. The structural tailwind is the rising total-loss rate (ADAS repair complexity) mechanically enlarging the salvage pool. The near-term reality is an air pocket, not a rebound: 9M FY26 revenue -0.2%, net +0.1% (Q1 +11.5% erased by Q2 -9.5%), so FY26 is rebuilt bottom-up on actuals (EPS ~1.65$, +3.8%, carried mostly by the buyback: 43.4M shares retired over 9M at ~37$). The 2027-2030 ramp is deliberately gradual (+4/+6/+7/+7.5%) and the buyback glide moderated (900 -> 550M$/yr) to reflect new CEO Adair's signaled capital diversification toward M&A - the single most sensitive assumption for 2027+.

== THESIS READ ==
- Third consecutive flat quarter (Q3 FY26 net -1.0%): the insurance-volume air pocket is confirmed cyclical-but-persistent; no rebound assumed before FY27.
- EPS growth is currently a buyback story (+3.8% on flat net) - fine while the moat holds pricing, but watch the M&A-vs-buyback arbitration under Adair.
- Purple Wave re-accelerated (+25% GTV) after the tariff-uncertainty dip flagged at Q2 - improvement read, not inconsistency.
- Interest income is real and growing (cash 5.5 -> 10.8bn$ modeled): the bridge carries it explicitly (+257 -> +663M$ at ~T10y+2pts), unlike zero-yield peers - Copart's buyback lacks the 2-3yr regularity that E5 a-bis requires for the zero branch.
- Watch: FY26 results (09/09) replace the whole bottom-up reconstruction - first full point under Adair.

== SPECIAL FACTORS ==
None.

== PARAMETERS & WATCH-LIST ==
Base: published US GAAP. Bridge (c-ter): t=20% flat (ETR normative), finNet = average net cash x ~T10y+2pts (ancrage resultatFinancierNet) - chain reconciles exactly; published FY25 reconciles at +243M$ interest. W1 flags the +17pt projected conversion rise (87% -> 104%): it is the INTEREST line compounding on a doubling cash pile, documented here, not a margin assumption. Scorecard: never guides - anchor own_vintage 1.65$ (24/07, near FY close; pose the FY27 anchor at the September results), history not measurable, application suspended. WATCH-LIST: (a) FY26 actuals (09/09); (b) Adair capital allocation (M&A vs buyback) - drives 2027+ EPS; (c) US insurance-volume inflection (still absent after 3 quarters); (d) total-loss rate trend; (e) international acceleration. Next useful refresh: FY26 results (09/09/2026).

== CATALYSTS ==
FY26 results (09 Sep): full-year actuals + Adair's first strategic frame; insurance-volume stabilization; total-loss secular tailwind; accretive buybacks on a depressed stock.

ancrages.moteur: FY2026 rebuilt bottom-up on the 9 months ACTUALLY reported (revenue -0,2% y/y, net income +0,07% y/y) + a reasoned Q4 (+1,5% revenue, +5% net income vs Q4 FY25, absent an identified catalyst) - replaces a top-down growth assumption (+5,9%) that was not consistent with the figures already published at the time of creation.

Gradual revenue growth 2027-2030 (+4%/+6%/+7%/+7,5%) replacing the previous assumption of an immediate rebound to +7-8% as early as 2027 - a flat FY26 does not justify a sharp rebound without an identified catalyst; the recovery is modelled as progressive, to be confirmed quarter after quarter.
Operating margin stable to slightly rising (36,7% in 2026 towards 37,8% in 2030, +0,2-0,3pt/yr), consistent with the operating leverage of the model once volumes have stabilised.

No debt and net cash >5 Md$. The buyback programme only started in Q2 FY2026 after $0 of buyback over FY2021-FY2025 (verified) - it does not meet the 'pace observed over at least the last 2-3 fiscal years' criterion of the E5-a-bis rule, so the zero yield does not apply. Branch retained: 10-year Treasury + 2pts (4,70% at 23/07/2026 + 2pts = 6,70%) on the average net cash of each PROJECTED year (2027-2030), iterative calculation. FY2026 (75% already published) does NOT use this synthetic methodology - rebuilt bottom-up on the actual results (see fy26BottomUp).

MODERATE buyback glide for 2027-2030 (900/700/600/550 M$, against 1300/1000/850/750 in the previous version) reflecting Jay Adair's explicit signal (call of 06/07/2026) of redirecting capital towards M&A (with debt flexibility) and organic investment (3 pillars), on top of buybacks - the future buyback pace is no longer guaranteed at the Q2-Q3 FY26 level. Average execution price assumed to rise (45$/50$/55$/60$) as the stock re-rates with the thesis, net of the dilution from share-based compensation (~8 M shares/yr).

FY2026: 43,4 M shares / >1,6 Md$ already bought back over 9 months (average price ~37$) + an estimated ~500 M$ more in Q4 (vs ~1,1 Md$ in Q3 alone - slowdown assumed given Adair's capital diversification signal). FY26 weighted average shares recalculated directly from the actual published quarterly EPS/net income (984,6 M / 972,1 M / 935,8 M in Q1/Q2/Q3, ~925 M estimated in Q4) rather than estimated top-down.

hypothese.cagrBridge: EPS CAGR ≈ +11.6%/yr over 2026-2030 (1,65$ -> 2,56$): FY2026 is now a transition year close to flat (net income +1,3%, EPS +3,8% driven almost entirely by the reduction in the share count already executed over 9 months), followed by a gradual acceleration from 2027 (revenue +4% -> +7,5%/yr, margin +0,2-0,3pt/yr, moderate buybacks given the capital diversification signalled by the new CEO). The 2026->2027 EPS jump (+15%) reflects the full-year benefit of the share base already reduced in 2026, NOT a sudden rebound in profitability. No dividend paid, so EPS CAGR = expected total return before any change in multiple. This trajectory depends heavily on assumptions not guaranteed by management (buyback pace, timing of the cyclical recovery) - to be treated as a central scenario, not a certainty.
